reviews.text: Star Trek Voyager was the first show I watched when I was a kid, it is what I was introduced to. When I booted into the main menu and heard the theme song, I was hit by a wave of nostalgia, I just sat and listened to it for a few minutes. It’s really nice to play a modern Star Trek game that isn't built for mobile or filled with $50 microtransactions for a new ship, it feels like a real game and you can tell the developers tried to put their heart in it. The What If? scenarios are really nicely done. My only real problem is the lack of full voice acting, which I understand the lack of, I do hope they add more in future updates to truly bring the crew to life. The biggest issue in general is the lack of saving, the autosaves are kind of sporadic but it was intentionally done to avoid people save scumming because of bad RNG, which is understandable but it does alienate a large portion of the user base of older adults who need to stop at a moments notice. The developers, however, are working on changing the saving to be more friendly to the players, it might be a while though to implement it. It has it's rough edges and it's by no means perfect but I am really looking forward to playing this and see what they do with it in the future. It runs pretty fantastically on the Steam Deck, Built in controller support, My game did freeze up while placing a room though which made me lose a few minutes of progress. Turns out if you try to move your cursor while placing the room it freezes and you can only open the menus then restart. Also, Janeway did not do anything wrong, Tuvix wasn't a person. Edit: After playing it for an hour, I understand the lack of voice acting, with the myriad of different pathes and alternate decisions, I think voice acting everything would be expensive to say the least. Though it would be nice to have occasional voice lines put in, other than Paris's cutscene at the beginning.

This one hurts. I’ve been desperately looking for a good Star Trek game. Something. Anything. A good RPG. A good simulator. A good strategy. I saw this game and saw the simulator part, the role playing part, the strategy part. It seemed to have all the things I wanted in a game like this. Until I started playing it. I hate to do this and again I wish there was a neutral button. But in this particular case, with this particular price tag I have to give it a thumbs down. It’s just not worth 35 dollars. There’s 98% no voice acting. The sound effects are sparse. The music is great though. The gameplay is slow and repetitive. The UI is needlessly confusing. There’s too much information and yet not enough direction. The ship battles are super fast, not enough to time to actually enjoy them. The away team missions are just text missions with RNG and super boring. The writing is sub par. Honestly the game is just average. I’m sure Star Trek fans will get a kick out of this, but only them. And even for them, I’d recommend a big discount. I just can’t find a single reason why this would be worth more than 25 dollars at the most. It’s an average game I guess. But I just don’t feel like it’s worth it. If you’d like more in-depth information with actual video footage then I encourage you to check out the review on my YouTube Channel (link below). https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CF7GzO0YW7k Otherwise, thanks so much for reading all this and I hope I was able to help some of you out there spend your money wisely.

I hate to do this as I am a diehard Star Trek fan and I really wish there was a star system for ranking, but with how the game is currently and with this particular price tag, I have to give it a thumbs down. It's just not worth $50 CAD. There’s almost no voice acting in the game and while the logs from Tom and Tuvok are great additions, the space combat voice acting is on par with Spider-Man 2. The sound effects aren't bad but there isn't much of them besides phasers, torpedos and the UI pinging. The gameplay thusfar is extremely boring. It feels like nothing actually happens. I'm surprised that the ship battles weren't too bad as seeing them in the trailers was worrysome but they are again, just a click this, press 1, 2 or 3 and sit and watch. The UI is essentially a clicking simulator with a bunch of (and sometimes random) information all over the place that is redundant or goes nowhere. The away team missions are literally just text boxes and an RNG simulation. Don't like the outcome? Just save scum it and do it over. There's really no reason not to do that. Unfortunately, the writing is really rough. They use some of the scripts from some of the episodes but even then, it rarely matches up with the show at all when it's supposed to. All in all, I'd say this game is a 2.5/5. It visually looks great and there is always the drive of the "What if..." scenario but that's the extent of the appeal presented. Some Star Trek fans will really enjoy this game and that's great! Realistically, I don't think there's any reasons as to why this game has the price point that it does. At most, I would put this at a $30 CAD game price. Should this go on sale for more than 30% off, I may revisit it again just to play with the story. Otherwise, I would recommend playing the Star Trek Stellaris mods or even the new Star Trek Armada 4 mod for Sins 2. They're more engaging and have much more to do than click and watch.

Overall: Not Recommended ❌ "We have heard you - very loudly..." but apparently, you weren't listening. I am writing this because the latest developer update regarding the saving mechanism is nothing short of a bureaucratic insult to the players' time. The developers claim that implementing a basic "Save on Quit" or manual save feature is "complicated" and might diminish "crucial game design decisions." Let’s be clear: Losing hours of progress due to real-life interruptions is not a 'design decision'; it is a technical failure. The Core Issues: Total Lack of 'Save on Quit': In 2026, it is inexcusable for a modern title to lack a basic "Exit and Save" function. This isn't "hardcore"—it's archaic. Disrespect for Player Time: The developers seem to believe that forcing players to hunt for specific checkpoints creates "immersion." In reality, it just creates resentment when you have to leave for work, a meal, or a system crash. Tone-Deaf PR: The recent announcement is a textbook example of "corporate word salad." It offers high emotional value ("our ears are ringing") but zero functional value. Acknowledging a problem without providing a timeline or a concrete solution is just stalling. Verdict: If you value your time and expect a baseline level of respect from a developer, stay away from this "unknown" until they figure out the most "known" feature in gaming history: The Save Button.

This is a really mixed bag.... and for those nostalgic for the pre-Kurtzman (and its various offshoots) era of Trek there's things to like about this... but there's areas which are very disappointing. First of all there's no excuse for Day 1 DLC. I am fed up of companies chopping bits out of games and flogging it to us for extra and calling it deluxe / premium etc. Either stick it in the main game or hang fire and release it later in a proper expansion / base game upgrade. The way this comes across is deluxe = "full game", base game = "hobbled a bit" and the difference is a tenner. Secondly the sound. It's nice to hear Tuvok and Paris (kudos for the developers for getting the actors to do the voiceovers) and the Voyager music on the title screen is a treat but the in-game effects are just... non existent. I'm not talking about lack of in-game voice overs (I got sucked into the gameplay enough at stages not to care) but when Voyager is travelling between planets, where's the roar of the engines? where's some half decent battle music when you enter into combat with the Kazon? There's just this constant ambient music. (But I do like the sounds for the individual rooms on Voyager when they're zoomed in on, again, a nice touch!) Third. No save on exit? That's a real issue. Fourth: Game overs. Really disappointing. Mutiny - you see some text. Ship gets destroyed - you see some text. Hull breaks apart - you see some text. If I'm going to fail then I'd least like to mark the occasion in a spectacular fashion. On the plus side the graphics do capture the characters and the feel of the show pretty well. Seeing Voyager zip between planets really does have that feel of exploration. Zooming into individual rooms on Voyager and seeing characters do their thing is a nice touch, the combat (which is token, and not that good, but you can see what they were going for) brings back memories of those Trek starship dogfights. And yes, having the opportunity to play the story, and make different decisions and seeing those characters again is a real attraction (although you can't be too much of an ass because it annoys the crew and morale is a complete pain in this game. The rank and file were never this finickity during those 7 seasons). The gameplay is where I'm in two minds. Scanning planets and collecting resource is just as tedious as it was in Mass Effect. Click on a planet to scan it. Zip over there (hoping you've enough fuel to keep the lights on) and be met with some options. 1) Leave the resource alone or 2) safe option to get a modest amount or 3) get some resources the risky way and try and fill yer cargo holds. Then it's over to the RNG to decide how successful you are. Same deal with the away missions. Choose your crew, beam down to a story scenario, and pick the member of your team to deal with a dilemma. Over to the RNG again. It'd be nice for some interactivity - have crew members make recommendations, hide the rng, make it more of an encounter where you're balancing crew ability, evaluating their recommendations against the demands of the situation. You could argue that's been done here, but it's horribly gamified. A missed opportunity. The ship combat? There really needs to be more options and more player agency. It doesn't have to be Starfleet Command - but there's very little sense of involvement. For those with long memories it's barely on par with the ship combat in Spectrum Holobytes "Star Trek: A Final Unity" - and no, that's not a compliment. And there's the time management. Yor fuel runs out in X cycles, build this thing in Y cycles, morale will collapse in Z cycles - all this while trying to accomplish the story missions which, to their credit, allow you to completely break canon but also can sting you with some nasty penalties if you fail them. There is a side of me that wished for more sandbox-type stuff and a greater sense of discovery. There's a lot of clicking around the map for resources before the next story mission crops up. So look, I like the atmosphere and the graphics, pretty decent job, the nostalgia kick is a win and 'rebuilding Voyager' is a nice management style element. But the sound is atrociously dull with too much of the gameplay left to chance, and, in the case of resource collection - too repetitive. At it's heart this is a pretty nice looking Trek game with overused RNG gameplay. It's quite easy to lose track of factors that will break your run. Collapses of morale can seem ridiculously unfair, once my hull broke apart and it wasn't clear as the reason why. The crew get antsy if you don't move forward fast enough If I was to recommend it, it would be for the nostalgia kick only, and that decent modern Trek games are hard to come by. But that's not enough. Having seen interviews with the devs I think they gave this a pretty good shot... and there's things they really do get right. But that ambient sound and overuse of RNG gameplay kills it. Sorry.

Captain’s log, Stardate 48315.6. The USS Voyager has found itself nostalgically stranded in the Delta Quadrant and it has fallen to me, Captain Katheryn Janeway, to guide the ship and its crew home. To do so we are steadily moving through sectors of space. Each sector is made up of a small number of systems each. Within each system are a number of harvestable resources, which is excellent news because they happen to be exactly the resources Voyager needs to continue to function. The Delta Quadrant will be bone dry by the time we make it home. Our primary concern is Deuterium which acts as our fuel. Without it the warp core would go dark and we would lose all power to our systems. As such, we must carefully manage our supply and continue to harvest and trade to keep our supply stocked. Occasionally I have had to cut power to certain sections just to keep us from becoming stranded. Harry Kim did not appreciate spending a week sleeping in a corridor because his quarters had no power. But if he didn’t want to be treated that way, he should have thought of that before he chose to stay an Ensign his entire life. Thankfully the warp core can be upgraded, so more power has become available as our journey continues. Luckily, Duranium & Tritanium are another pair of materials the Delta Quadrant has in abundance. We use these materials to build additional rooms on each deck of the ship. What we build and where it is placed is dictated primarily by me. Does Mr. Tuvok appreciate having his shield control room next to Neelix’s Mess Hall? Luckily I don’t know or care, because I am the Captain and the crew will build whatever wherever I decree. The resource which has caused the most trouble onboard so far? Food. The crew are endless devouring machines, filling their bellies faster than we can replicate food. I have commissioned the building of four hydroponics bays (yes, four!) in an attempt to grow enough food for them, but our output pales in comparison to their hunger. They will simply not stop eating! So far I am managing to keep these bottomless pits fed through intermittent use of replicators, which depletes our precious Deuterium. It is possible at this rate we will fail to make it home to Earth simply because the crew won’t stop eating through our fuel… Another resource we make use of is less tangible, science points. We accumulate science points through our workshops and occasionally through studying local planets. These points we then spend on research projects which can improve many different aspects of the ship. The options of which technology to research are laid out for me in a tree-like menu, a tech tree if you will. We have encountered a number of hostile ships on our journey so far, though perhaps less than I had expected. Combat is mostly automated based on the systems I have built, though I still maintain enough control to occasionally tell three members of the crew to perform certain manoeuvres. Although, they do not like it when I do this, so I have to give them 15 seconds or so to calm down before I can tell them to do it again. If I try to tell them before their “cooldown” period, they ignore me. At the very least I can tell the crew which area of the enemy ship to focus on, and which area of our ship needs protecting. Meanwhile, we have performed numerous away missions. I have selected what I believe to be the appropriate crew each time, although we can only fit 3 of them on the transporter pad per mission. This is probably because, as previously noted, the crew will not stop eating. Presumably they have ballooned to Star Trek V era Scotty levels of roundness, making it hard to find room on the transporter pad for more than 3. During away missions I have been prompted to make several choices based on a probability matrix of success. Sometimes the numbers fall in our favour, sometimes they do not and Tuvok is left lungless. I shouldn’t laugh, but have you ever seen a Vulkan attempt to remain smug without lungs? I have. It tastes sweeter than the finest replicated coffee. Unsurprisingly, there is a lot of talking involved in navigating the Delta Quadrant. Like our away missions, these conversations with ships we encounter often involve choosing between a small handful of alternate options. How I choose to respond sometimes leads to rewards, and other times to consequences… especially when I can’t fully remember the episode that’s being referenced so I choose wrongly and make everybody onboard mad at me. Speaking of upsetting the crew, a morale meter measures their happiness with me and our mission. I have noticed the crew grow restless and rude if I order us to remain in a sector too long. This gives our journey a sense of urgency even when I just want to fly us around in a circle and make sure we’ve not missed any opportunities to find food for my fickle gluttonous crew. Altogether the journey so far is a very enjoyable one. Managing materials has kept me engaged throughout, and the variety of activities feels perfectly balanced. I really do feel like a Starfleet captain. In conclusion, I am pleased I have been sucked into the Delta Quadrant and I look forward to more adventures to come. I highly recommend the experience. Captain’s Log Supplemental: Yes, I chose to murder Tuvix and I would do it again.

There's a game in here somewhere. Hopefully, they will find it. This is an incompletely developed game. Why this game was released without being ready can only be chalked up to some deadline setting know-nothing executive. I bought this game because I am a Star Trek fan, especially Voyager, and want to promote the production of any game set in the Star Trek world... when Star Trek was still good... There are a few glaring problems that I can only hope the makers of this game will fix in rolling updates. I would love to see this concept brought to a playable state. 1. The save system is a nightmare. Not much to say here, it's full of bugs and I don't think they even know how they want it to function yet. 2. Game progression is hinged on a random 50/50 outcome of every action. You can lose the game through no fault of your own simply by a few bad rolls. 3. No Game mechanics tutorial. You can, and most likely will, fail the tutorial because the game spends the intro teaching you the interface and NOT the game mechanics. Hopefully, it won't take more than a couple of shots for you to figure out resource management and gathering. 4. Ship status alerts and presets. This is supposed to be a Star Trek game… where are my status alerts?!. Having to manually switch individual systems on and off constantly takes me out of the actual game and makes me want to simply stop playing. It isn’t fun. Again, I want this game to succeed. I want this game to be fun. Neither is currently the case. So, I’ll shelve it for a year while the dev’s do what they were supposed to do. I blame the imbecile who pushed the deadline and released an unfinished, barely playable and un-fun game. That said, more classic Star Trek games please :)

This game is both very fun and incredibly, incredibly frustrating. To put it simply it's incredibly RNG dependent, and the odds are very punishing. You can do absolutely fine, have everything topped off and upgrade all your equipment and then a series of bad rolls mean you have to restart an entire sector because you're in a literally unwinnable situation. The Good: The game captures a lot of the visuals, spirit, and enjoyment of Voyager. It can be fun to manage logistics and upgrade your ship. Some of the "alternate history" moments are neat as well, and you can get a lot of crew that never existed on the show. The Bad: There are a fair few bugs. For instance, during one point in the game two crew members are getting sucked into a black hole. In spite of successfully beaming one of them off the ship, both were treated as dead. Why? No idea. As a result I lost Be'lanna and Tom Paris in a single mission. Some dialogue options are also pointless. For instance, I got a rare healing device thanks to good RNG, and I can trade tech to get enemies off my back. This device is one of the options - yet it's just refused. So why even bother including it? I didn't get any other RNG-based cool tech, so my only option was to slug it out. RNG is absolutely atrocious. You can upgrade your facilities and have a constant 10-20% failure on rolls anyway, meaning you'll likely fail 1-5 of every normal thing, losing crew, taking ship damage, and getting no resources. Voyager had its issues but it didn't constantly have crew dying every time they went to get food. The combat can also be frustrating. Have 3 level 2 shield generators? Some enemies will just one-shot through them somehow anyway and when you select "defend port" or whatever, the ship might turn, or might not. If you have multiple shields down it's impossible to just get the side of the ship to face the enemy that you want to face the enemy. You can also have rooms get damaged during combat. For instance, I had a mission where I needed an upgraded holodeck. I flew into a sector, got into a fight with two enemies and the ship wouldn't defend properly against two opponents so I took some damage to the ship. What got damaged? The holodeck of course, so I was left with two 40% options that failed. The morale is also utterly crushing. The game is constantly pushing you forward with massive morale drops even when you've got every morale tech you can up and the mission isn't done. Stay one second too long in a sector? Suddenly the crew is brawling and looking for your head. On the transwarp system sector I went from 100% full to two 0 morale game over checks because the main mission is long and the crews patience is not. All of this was playing on the normal difficulty. I strongly recommend playing on the easiest difficulty until you know the game inside and out and basically plan around the mandatory story checks, because you'd have to be psychic to actually get the game right on the first try. If you get to a section of the game and don't have the right upgrades, you just lose. Get a series of bad rolls, you just lose. Get a bad system layout or take the wrong room damage at the wrong time, and you just lose. I find this game fun in many respects but it has a lot of flaws that need fixing and it desperately needs rebalancing, more missions, and far more bonuses for upgrading your systems. When level 1 engineering bays or whatever and level 2 ones both have a 5-10% chance of blowing up your ship on routine missions it's absolute BS. In its current state I can't recommend it - I find the RNG far more frustrating than Darkest Dungeon, and there are many times I find myself loudly cussing at the screen because RNG just utterly screwed me over and made the game unwinnable when I did nothing wrong. If you compared the difficulty of the actual show with this game, they played on a modded ultra-easy mode where they started with most of their ship intact and heavily upgraded. Also, RNG came up in their favor almost every single time.

If you like Voyager and thought you could do better than Janeway you should give this game a try. It may take a failure or two to get the hang of things and you might get bad RNG but clearing a sector and upgrading the ship is very rewarding. It has sort of a Fallout 1 difficultly feel (but with autosaves) mixed with some fallout shelter layout and an Oregon Trail in space vibe. It is very resource focused not so much a space battle game. A few bad choices can be crippling and have you fleeing to scrounge for resources. You'll be wishing there were some buffalo to hunt in the Delta quadrant. 7.5/10 (although I guess I could be generous and round up my ratting to 7/9)

What to say about this game. I wanted to enjoy it; being a HUGE Star Trek fan - and I think that's what kept me playing for 10+ hours, but unfortunately that wore thin after a while. There is no strategy here, there is no influence; except where you want to go to - or not go to depending how low your resources are. This is my list of Pros and Cons Pros - Nostalgia... That is about it. Cons - It is TOTALLY RANDOM; you might as well have an electronic dice button, or guess what number the computer is thinking, as that is all you can influence when it comes to collecting resources. Not fun. - It is point and click, and I get they added a manual save option (because others complained at the difficulty), but all that made me do was move, save, role dice and either continue or reload save. I honestly watched the arrow hover over the green area, and then with less than a second to go swing right to the red, resulting in damage, death or destruction. Not fun - Resources are so limited. Three, of the seven, play throughs I had lacked one resources, which meant I could not upgrade my warp core, which meant my shields, weapons and crew were lacking, meaning space battles were short... and usually to my destruction. Not fun - I get it is a resource management game, but the ship goes through so many resources, I am amazed that Voyager made it home at all in the TV show, if they went by the games resource mechanics here they wouldn't have made it 100 light years. Resource management means having to constantly balance crew morale, energy, food, fuel etc. Not fun. - Action. This is a story game, nothing more, and I dare say if you wanted the story then just watch the TV show. Space battles... press either 1, 2 or 3 to influence a hero, but that is it. You control nothing more than that. Not fun. There is probably a few more cons I could highlight, but the above were my biggest issues. I never made it past season 4 (Level 4) as the constant resource heavy management, and it is heavy, often had me reload the random number generator mechanic when it looked like I was going to get the precious resources I needed to fuel the ship or repair the hull and then watch it zoom right into the red and either kill or injure a crew member, destroy a shuttle, damage the ship, or if I was lucky just not get the resource at all. Review by [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/34633003-Gaming-Masterpieces/lists/] Gaming Masterpieces [/url] - The greatest games of all time on Steam. Is this game a masterpiece? Nah, but you are the captain! In this case, the captain of the U.S.S. Voyager, responsible for every aspect of the massive starship on its adventures in the depths of space. And this alone is rather cool, even if the game has a few limitations. Personally, I’m more of a fan of the original Star Trek episodes, but Star Trek: Voyager, which aired from 1995 to 2001 with a total of 172 episodes, also has a considerable fan base. And it is within this part of the Star Trek universe that the new game is set. There have been quite a few Star Trek computer games over the years, but only a handful have become true hits. My favorites are still the older MS-DOS point-and-click adventures Star Trek: 25th Anniversary and Star Trek: Judgment Rites, as well as the real-time strategy game Star Trek: Armada. However, this new game leans more toward starship simulations like Bridge Commander, Starfleet Command, or Star Trek: Legacy. So what does Star Trek: Voyager – Across the Unknown offer? The announced mix of a survival game and a starship simulator certainly sounds promising. Let’s head into the Delta Quadrant! At the start, you choose the difficulty level. You can select between Adventure, Survival, and Years of Hell, which influence resource availability, the difficulty of combat and missions, as well as your crew’s homesickness. You take on the role of Captain Kathryn Janeway, commanding the Voyager. Harry Kim, Tom Paris, B’Elanna, Tuvok, and other familiar crew members stand by your side when, during a mission in the Badlands, the Voyager is suddenly thrown 70,000 light-years across space and reappears as a wreck in the (procedurally generated) Delta Quadrant. Will you ever make it back home? This is where the game begins: you scan nearby planets for resources—deuterium, duranium, tritanium—for fuel, repairs, and reconstruction. You travel there and choose from several options for your approach. Safe but low yield, or risky with potentially higher rewards? The choice is yours. The Voyager consists of countless stations—from the warp core to crew quarters, bio-labs, cargo bays, transporter room, engineering, sickbay, bridge, shield generator, torpedo room, shuttle bay, holodeck, cafeteria, and much more. You decide which rooms to repair or rebuild and how each station operates. Emergency rations or full meals? What should research focus on? Where should your construction teams be deployed? For missions outside the Voyager, you first choose up to three crew members, beam them to the location, and then decide how they should proceed based on their feedback. The game shows the level of risk for each choice, and the outcome is then essentially “rolled.” Progress is presented through text and small images. After several decisions, most missions conclude, and your (surviving) crew members return to the Voyager. Meanwhile, you must manage food, fuel, battery levels, and crew morale, research new technologies, and gradually rebuild the (initially heavily damaged) Voyager as you explore sector after sector of the Delta Quadrant. You’ll fight enemies in hectic space battles using lasers and torpedoes (you issue commands, your crew executes them in real time), and send small teams on away missions. You’ll encounter Borg, Klingons, and other species—and hope the game doesn’t end up in a soft-lock situation where you can do nothing but return to the main menu. Unfortunately, that happened to me twice during testing. Since the game autosaves regularly, it’s annoying, but not a disaster. Graphically, Star Trek: Voyager – Across the Unknown offers 4K support, menus styled after the series, and well-made cutscenes—but not jaw-dropping, cinematic visuals during actual gameplay. You jump between side-view ship sections, navigate countless menus, and experience away missions through text supported by still images. The outcomes of your crew’s actions are… well, largely determined by chance. Your odds of success improve with the right preparation, but ultimately a random number generator decides the result. With bad luck, even important crew members can die quickly. There are no “redshirts” (the expendable characters from classic Star Trek). The story is varied and complex—Star Trek: Voyager – Across the Unknown is a great narrative experience, but not a graphical showcase. What also immediately stood out to me is the lack of elaborate sound design. There’s some series music and a few basic sound effects, but no full voice acting. You’ll be reading a lot of text with very little spoken dialogue. Of course, fully voicing all that text (potentially in multiple languages, possibly even with original voice actors) would be a massive undertaking. Still, the audio presentation is not one of the game’s highlights. Its strengths lie in its complex ship simulation and non-linear storytelling—not in its presentation. [u][b] Conclusion:[/b][/u] Star Trek: Voyager – Across the Unknown is a complex simulation of the (initially nearly destroyed) U.S.S. Voyager. You take on the role of captain, deciding which rooms to rebuild and how to allocate scarce resources while scanning unknown planets for materials and completing frequent story-driven missions. You regularly face multiple-choice decisions, with success probabilities shown beforehand. Detailed overview screens display the status of your starship. This is not a game for “fair-weather captains”—it requires some time to understand the interplay of its many systems and to make informed decisions. However, if you enjoy that—and appreciate the Star Trek atmosphere—there is currently no better way to step into Kathryn Janeway’s shoes and guide the U.S.S. Voyager through the Delta Quadrant. Will you manage to bring the Voyager safely back home?

I really wanted to like this game. I read a lot of the negative reviews and figured it was just the usual. Having played it now I kinda get where other people are coming from. I've enjoyed my time with the game so far. The story follows the entire Voyager TV series, but with a twist: Events don't necessarily have to play out the same way. The core gameplay is about resource management and XCOM-style base building. Voyager is badly damaged during the intro. You have work crews onboard who can be assigned to repair damaged rooms, clear debris to make open space, and build new rooms or upgrade existing ones. You have to run around collecting resources in between events to keep the ship running as you make the long journey home across the galaxy. The other main gameplay elements are ship battles, away missions, and shipboard story events. Space combat is semi-automatic where you manage the ship's power levels and designate targets. Hero characters each have a special space combat ability that can be used on a cooldown. During away missions, each hero character on the team will have two or three skill ratings in various disciplines (science, engineering, security, command, diplomacy, medicine), as well as some semi-unique traits (pilot, etc.). These skills and traits are what determine your available options and chances for success. The game is highly randomized, so you make most of your choices by playing the odds and weighing risk/reward. That can be irritating at times, but it does give it a little bit of a D&D feel to everything you do, albeit without dice. The style of game is a very good fit for Voyager, and if you want to relive the series, this is definitely worth a look.

Voyager: Across the ... Unfinished After an entire playthrough, to keep it short and a bit bitter: As a Star Trek and Voyager fan, this game hints at excellence but ultimately plays like an unfinished board game. On a technical note, the lore is spot-on. But on a narrative and character level, it misses the mark so drastically that if you stripped away the Trek skin, it would feel a bit like the Alters minus Jan Dolski and everything that makes that game good. In Voyager, there is virtually no character development, and the overarching story is barely integrated into the design. Dialogue and event progression rely entirely on RNG dice rolls. Finally, to understand the game design is a simple equation of (Ant Farm) - (Ants) + (Xia: Legends of a Drift System) + (Nemesis) = (Voyager: Across the Unknown). Here's the thing, I'm not going to bash that design equation, this could still be fun. If, and only if, any visual or audio artistry were present in immersing you into the world or the story or something! But the presentation is incredibly barebones (despite what the trailer might lead you to believe) and the immersion into Star Trek is mostly ignored. The audio remains completely static regardless of story outcomes; there is no dynamic musical shift to match the stakes of what you are doing. A reactive soundtrack is the lowest-effort way to build immersion, yet it is entirely absent, amongst any other more complicated immersion tool. Frankly, the original Pokémon Red and Blue on the Game Boy handled narrative immersion and character stakes better. This failure is impossible to ignore because Voyager is inherently built for high-stakes drama -- it’s literally Homer's Odyssey in deep space, and they turned it into a spreadsheet. Compounding this, the combat is abhorrent -- a clunky, third-person view of the ship with minimal command controls and terrible graphics for a modern space battle. I’m giving it a thumbs-up solely for the concept and their ability to obtain the Star Trek license. The dual-layer gameplay mechanics between galaxy exploration and internal ship management are a great start, but the execution falls flat everywhere else. It didn't make me want to play more; it just made me want to rewatch the show, and apparently get a Paramount+ subscription -- was this the plan all along? This is an unreasonably priced unfinished indie title ($50 Retail) that completely ignored the most important parts of the franchise's allure. Unless you love point-and-click, dice-rolling grinds with zero narrative depth, pass. A short letter to the Developers, I don't want to be crass, but it feels like the momentum for this project entirely relied on securing the Star Trek license. You got the technical lore right -- which is great -- but for a Trek fanbase, that is the bare minimum. But forget about the Trek fanbase for a second, if you had attempted even a single interesting choice regarding immersion, combat, or character depth, this would be a completely different review and monetary outcome (because I'd recommend it to every single one of my friends). Instead, the game either played it too safe, or the budget was entirely drained paying for the IP rights. If there are actual Star Trek fans on your team, I have to ask: where was the love? Ultimately, the game felt the most like Voyager on the title screen, right before hitting "Start."

The game is fun and the basic gameplay loop is satisfying and I really want to recommend it to others, but I can't right now. Primarily because some developer decisions just seem downright lazy. For example: In my playthrough I ended up with the separated Klingon and Human versions of B'Elanna Torres. It wasn't the outcome I wanted, but I decided to play through with that outcome in the spirit of this game as a "what if?" retelling of the Voyager story. Presumably that's as the developers intended to play this game. I'm cool with that. What was very disappointing and feels downright lazy from developers is that because I no longer have the original B'Elanna Torres on my crew, my Chief Engineer for the rest of the game is now replaced by the generic "Lieutenant Lani" who isn't even a usable Hero. Why the heck is my main engineer not either of the two versions of B'Elanna I have on my crew? Or for that matter why not even Joe Carey, who I have as a Hero? It feels very unimmersive and lazy that I'm now stuck with a generic character as my Chief Engineer in a HUGE number of game dialogs for the rest of the game. Easy fixes would be either: a) Let us choose any hero as senior staff officer (how fun would it be to make someone random and non-canon, like Kunut, Chief of Security for example? or Telek R'Mor as Chief Science Officer?) b) if the starting Hero who was a senior staff member is lost, it defaults to the next Hero with the highest relevant skill. So when I lost the Klingon-Human B'Elanna, it would've defaulted to Carey or Human B'Elanna as Chief Engineer. Just seems like a glaring oversight from the developers of this game and makes the whole experience feel rushed and disappointing. Especially since neither of these seems like difficult game development implementations — it's just a matter of swapping out names and profile images in those dialogs. This is just one example that really upset me and basically took the joy out of the game for me. Hopefully developers fix this and other similar issues to make the game more fun, because there's the framework for a really great game here and I want to keep support it with the expansions — *IF* they fix this sort of thing.

The Good: This is a game that works in 'seasons' that randomize Voyager storylines and allows most of them to be completed in alternative ways. Credit to the devs, Voy was the beginning of the end for Trek writing quality Janeway was a tyrant that made alot of sh***y decisions, you're at least allowed to make better choices and most quests feature branches that lead to fan theorized alternative story resolutions. Also, VOY was originally marketed as a survial adventure about a ship stranded far beyond support and supply lines, which due to poor writing was seldom felt on screen. This game gets the resource management aspect right at least. So why is there a negative review? Because there's one huge story/writing failure that drags the experience down and stands out like a sore thumb: Huge Turnoff: Main VOY characters can die and minor characters can be promoted throughout the course of the story. In theory if B'elanna Torres were to die, a promoted Joe Carey should have been able to run engineering and to pick up her speaking role through the remaining speaking role. Unfortunately the developers took the worst options; whenever an established character leaves the crew the game designates a generic no-name character to deliver the exact same dialogue as the character that could have potentially been dead for the majority of the game's playtime. The devs even snuck a second Talaxian for when the player inevitably opts to ditch the hedgehog Neelix for the far superior Tuvix. The writer's could and should have done better with having secondary characters be able to deliver relevant lines during storylines and only reserve the no-name standins for cases where there's literally nobody appropriate left in the crew to deliver the line. Also, several issues with mission requirements poorly integrated into the ship, A large hydroponics bay will not count as a small hydroponics bay when it comes to meeting requirements for special dialogue options, leaving the player forced to maintain several redundant systems to maximize mission outcomes.
